catalog_quote: Analyzing accent marks in Li’s materials reveals a preference for penultimate stress in Wailaki. Li’s description of Wailaki stress is consistent with an analysis whereby penultimate stress is preferred if one assumes heavy stems still have penultimate stress, even if word-final on the surface, due to the presence of an underlying relative enclitic, or another enclitic, which may often be deleted. Li also writes an accent mark over syllables in other positions on occasion, but the predominant pattern is penultimate stress. [p. 66] ... Instead of a two-syllable window, a preference for penultimate stress in shown in Table 14. ... For each length, the proportion that has penultimate stress is at least 65%. For words that are two syllables long, overwhelmingly 272 tokens of 322 (84.5%) have stress exclusively on the first syllable. For words that are three syllables long, 440 of 533 (82.6%) have stress on the second syllable. For words that are four syllable long, 245 of 329 (74.5%) on the third syllable. For words that are five syllables long, 93 of 136 (68.4%) the fourth syllable. Finally, for the 43 examples that are six and seven syllables long, though examples are scarce, the majority still fall on penultimate syllables – the fifth for six syllable words, and sixth for seven syllable words, respectively. Considered overall, however, the figure is higher: 79.6% ... Despite these outstanding questions, the preference for penultimate stress is clear in the data. [p. 68]
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls predominantly on the penultimate syllable (79.6% of 1363 stress-marked tokens in Li's 1927 notecards; two-syllable words 84.5% initial, three-syllable 82.6% second, four-syllable 74.5% third, five-syllable 68.4% fourth). Li's older rule (stress on the stem if heavy, on the syllable before the stem if light) is treated as penultimate stress with a deleted word-final enclitic. No lexical tone; Wailaki has a stress system.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described as such; about 1.5% of tokens are 'double marked' (two accent marks, on two prefixes or a prefix and the stem) and are left unexplained.
new_statements.exceptions: About 20% of tokens carry stress outside the penult; the conditioning factors (syllable weight, weight hierarchy, noun vs. verb) are explicitly left for further research. Phonetic correlates unknown since no recordings exist.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, based entirely on philological analysis of accent marks in Fang-Kuei Li's 1927 field notecards (431 cards, mostly verb paradigms and wordlist forms), i.e. citation/elicited forms of a dormant language; no acoustic data.
new_statements.identity_note: Begay 2018 uses 'Wailaki' as a cover term for the whole Eel River Athabaskan dialect continuum (Glottolog wail1244, ISO wlk; Golla 2011's Eel River Athabaskan, incl. Wailaki proper, Lassik, Nongatl, Sinkyone); the stress analysis rests on Li's 1927 data from Round Valley speakers (Wailaki proper). Cahto/Kato is a separate language and is not covered.

new_statements.quote: Li (1930:22) briefly considers Wailkai stress in his Mattole grammar. Li considered Wailaki to have a stress system rather than lexical tone, and wrote that an “accent mark in Hupa, Wailaki and Mattole denote stress” (Li 1930: 5). new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable. Stems that surface with final stress (heavy stems) are analysed as still penultimate because of an underlying (often deleted) enclitic. new_statements.identity_note: Begay 2018 describes Eel River Wailaki (Tsennahkennes), the most documented of the four regional Wailaki dialects; the stress counts come from Li Fang-Kuei's 1927 notecards from speaker John 'Wylakke' Tip, Round Valley Reservation. Li 1930 is a grammar of Mattole (Mattole-Bear River, a different Eel River Athabaskan language); only its pp. 5 and 22 comment on Wailaki.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the primary source behind the catalog record: Begay 2017 §2.7 quotes exactly these two passages (Li 1930: 5 and 22) and builds the penultimate analysis on them. Read directly, Li gives a stem-relative, stem-weight-conditioned rule (stem-stressed if heavy = surface-final; pre-stem if light = surface-penultimate), and confirms stress rather than lexical pitch. That is compatible with the catalog's 'fixed: penultimate' only under Begay's assumption that heavy (subordinate-clause) forms carry an underlying relative enclitic, an assumption Li's own p. 19 n. 2 (heavy form confined to subordinate clauses) supports; on the surface Li's rule yields final stress in heavy-stem verb forms, so t…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Li treats Wailaki (his own 1927 field material) as a stress-accent language, not a pitch/tone language (accent mark = stress, unlike Sarcee and Navaho where it marks pitch). His one placement statement for Wailaki is stem-relative and conditioned by the stem alternant: in verbs the accent falls on the stem syllable when the stem is in its heavy form and on the syllable immediately preceding the stem when the stem is in its light form (stated for nasal-final stems, where Wailaki has lost the segmental heavy/light contrast and the accent alone carries it). He adds that in Wailaki the light form is the general one and the heavy form is restricted to certain syntactic conditions such as subordinate clauses. Since the stem is normally the last syllable of the verb word, this amounts to final stress on heavy-stem (subordinate) forms and penultimate stress on light-stem forms. No general statement about nouns or about Wailaki word accent as a whole; no Wailaki section (Wailaki is a comparison language throughout).
new_statements.exceptions: Statement is explicitly limited ('in this case') to the nasal-final stem type; heavy forms occur 'only in certain syntactic conditions, for instance, in the subordinate clauses'; Li rejects Goddard's (Kato, pp. 17-18) explanation of the same facts while accepting the facts.
new_statements.identity_note: Li's Wailaki is his own 1927 Round Valley field material (Eel River Athabaskan, Wailaki proper), used as a comparison language in a grammar of Mattole (matt1238); the book has no Wailaki chapter, only comparative citations ('Wail.') and footnotes. Statements about Mattole accent (§ 56, pp. 50-51: weak accent, stem syllable = usually last, or the syllable preceding the stem; heavy verb stems always accented) belong to matt1238, not to this item.

readall_conflicts: No outright contradiction. Li 1930, read directly, states for Wailaki a stem-relative accent conditioned by the stem alternant (accent on the stem in the heavy form, on the syllable preceding the stem in the light form; stated for nasal-final stems) and that the accent is stress, not pitch. The catalog record (Begay 2017, fixed penultimate, grid penultimate stress) is Begay's reanalysis of exactly these Li passages plus Li's accent marks: penultimate throughout once heavy-stem (subordinate-clause) forms are given an underlying, often deleted, relative enclitic. On the surface Li's rule puts stress on the final (stem) syllable of heavy-stem verb forms, so a strictly surface coding from Li alone would be 'stem or pre-stem by stem weight' rather than a pure penult grid; Begay herself notes Li also marks accent on other syllables occasionally. The two existing statements held by the project (both from Begay, reading fixed penultimate) already paraphrase the p. 22 sentence correctly; 19 n. 2 remark that heavy forms are confined to subordinate clauses, which is the distributional fact Begay's enclitic analysis relies on.
